newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Opinion split on success of Romanian OTC system.
newsitem.headline: Opinion split on success of Romanian OTC system.

text.p: A month after the opening of Romania's over-the-counter (OTC) market, most brokers have welcomed growing volumes, but some say it is unfair competition for the stock exchange.
"We saw it as healthy competition for an ailing bourse, but confusing market regulator rules are forcing companies gone private to turn to it en masse," one broker said on Friday.

The RASDAQ trading system opened on October 25 as part of a capital market development project run by the U.S. Agency for International Development, rounding off Romania's budding capital market. The stock exchange opened last November.
The OTC system was designed eventually to trade shares in 5,000 companies, most turned over to private hands under a mass selloff which gave Romanians shares in exchange for coupons.

It started trading with six stocks, but has grown rapidly to 344 listings. This week, it saw a five-day turnover of 351.75 million lei, down from 376 million the previous week and equivalent to five weeks of bourse trading.
Bourse executives also complained about market regulator CNVM's rules, saying mass selloff companies had to sign up with the Romanian shareholders' registry.

They said that registry was compatible with the OTC market rather than the exchange, which keeps its own records. At least 200 of the 4,000 state companies on offer under the mass selloff could easily qualify for a bourse quotation, they say.
A CNVM official agreed the rules should have been amended long ago. "Some of us repeatedly asked for a revision of those rules. So far nothing happened," he told Reuters.
But brokers said many of the RASDAQ listed companies broke listing rules by failing to sign up with the registry.
Registry manager Mircea Ilie said companies could join the OTC system and then sign on.
"Companies can now sign with the registry later. This is intended to give Romanians a market for mass privatisation shares more quickly," he said.
